doc.title: Inside an LLM – from prompt to token
doc.description: An interactive multilingual course connecting LLM foundations and tensor operations to training, quantization, inference, evaluation and tool-enabled systems. Worked examples, visual experiments and practical serving exercises in one offline HTML file.
mod.0.name: Start
mod.1.name: The basics
mod.1.lead: Four tools used at every step of the model: vectors, matrix multiplication, non-linearity and softmax. Plus the most important distinction in the course.
mod.1.desc: Vectors, dot products, matmul, ReLU and softmax, plus weights versus activations.
mod.1.goal.1: read a shape like [T, 4096] and say what a matmul does with it
mod.1.goal.2: explain what a dot product measures and where it is used
mod.1.goal.3: explain why the model needs non-linearity
mod.1.key.1: A vector is a list of numbers. The dot product measures how much two vectors point in the same direction.
mod.1.key.2: x @ W: each output value is a dot product between x and a column of W. [T, d_in] @ [d_in, d_out] → [T, d_out], row by row.
mod.1.key.3: Without non-linearity between the layers, the whole model collapses into a single matrix.
mod.1.key.4: Softmax turns numbers into probabilities. Only the differences between logits matter.
mod.1.key.5: Weights are fixed and used every time: every weight matrix is read in full for every token, but embedding is instead a lookup of one row per token, as module 2 shows. Activations are computed per token and are what you study.
mod.2.name: Text → tokens
mod.2.lead: The model only computes with numbers. Here text becomes token ids, and ids become vectors.
mod.2.desc: Tokenizer, BPE, chat template and embedding.
mod.2.goal.1: explain why text is split into subword tokens
mod.2.goal.2: describe what a chat template does
mod.2.goal.3: state the shape before and after embedding
mod.2.key.1: The tokenizer turns text into ids from a fixed vocabulary: 128,256 tokens in Llama 3.
mod.2.key.2: The number of tokens, not words, drives cost, speed and how much fits in the context.
mod.2.key.3: Embedding is a table lookup: ids [T] → x [T, 4096].
mod.2.key.4: A chat template turns a conversation into a single string with special tokens for the roles.
mod.3.name: The block and the residual stream
mod.3.lead: The heart of the model: the same block 32 times, and a workspace per token that never changes shape.
mod.3.desc: The transformer block, residual stream, normalisation, parameters and shapes.
mod.3.goal.1: explain what a transformer, decoder-only and a block are
mod.3.goal.2: explain the residual stream and why the shape never changes
mod.3.goal.3: list the weights in a layer and their shapes
mod.3.goal.4: count the parameters in a layer and in the whole model
mod.3.goal.5: explain what attention and the MLP do and how they differ
mod.3.goal.6: follow Q, K and V through attention with the right shapes
mod.3.goal.7: explain causal mask, RoPE and GQA
mod.3.goal.8: count the parameters in one layer
mod.3.key.1: A decoder-only transformer is one block (attention + MLP) repeated L = 32 times, where each token only sees the tokens before it.
mod.3.key.2: The residual stream x is a workspace per token that every block reads from and adds to. Its shape [T, 4096] never changes until the LM head.
mod.3.key.3: Pre-norm: the blocks read a normalised copy, the stream itself is left to grow and is normalised once, before the LM head.
mod.3.key.4: A layer is 7 weight matrices and 2 norm weights, about 218 M parameters. All 32 layers share the shapes but not the values.

lead.vektorer-och-skalarprodukt: A vector is just a list of numbers, like a row in a spreadsheet. The dot product is a way to measure how similar two such lists are. It is the most common arithmetic step in the whole model.
lead.matris-ganger-vektor: A matrix is a table of numbers that turns one list into another list. It is the model’s basic arithmetic step, and almost all the time on a GPU goes into exactly this.
lead.varfor-icke-linjaritet: If the model only multiplied by tables, it could only draw straight lines. A small switch between the steps lets it shape any curve or rule.
lead.softmax: The model outputs ordinary numbers, but we want probabilities. Softmax turns the numbers into percentages that add up to 100.
lead.vikter-och-aktiveringar: The weights are the model’s knowledge: learned once and then fixed. The activations are the model’s thoughts about your particular text, and they are computed again every time.
lead.varfor-tokens: Computers work with numbers, not letters. So the text is first chopped into pieces, tokens, and each piece gets a number.
lead.embedding-fran-id-till: Each token number is looked up in a huge table and swapped for a list of 4096 numbers. That is the model’s first picture of the word.
lead.uppgiften-fran-vektorer-till: At first a word knows nothing about the words around it. The model’s job is to let the words share information, until the last position knows enough to guess the next word.
lead.transformer-och-decoder-only: “Transformer” is the blueprint for many modern language models, including the course’s Llama example, but not all. “Decoder-only” here reads text from left to right: each position uses itself and earlier tokens to predict the next one.
lead.ett-block-staplat-32-ganger: The model is the same building block repeated many times, like floors in a house. Each floor refines the understanding a little further.
lead.residual-stream: Every word has a notepad that travels with it through the whole model. Every layer reads it and adds a note, but never erases.
lead.shapen-andras-aldrig: The notepad has the same size all the way through the model. Only at the very end is it turned into one number per possible next word.
lead.normalisering-varfor-och-var: When you keep adding notes, the numbers grow larger and larger. Normalization scales them down to an even level before the next step reads them.
lead.hela-modellen-i-en-bild: Here all the parts are put together into one picture. This is the map for the rest of the module.
lead.ett-lager-inifran: Now we open up one layer and look at everything in it: nine sets of learned numbers and a few fixed calculation rules.
lead.32-lager-i-en-modellfil: A model file is a list of named tables of numbers. Here you see exactly which tables belong to each layer.
lead.rmsnorm: Here is the exact formula for the normalization: divide every number by the vector’s average size.
lead.attention-och-mlp-olika-jobb: The two parts of every layer have completely different tasks. Attention lets the words talk to each other, the MLP lets each word think on its own.
lead.gqa-delade-kv-heads: Storing all the labels and content costs memory. GQA lets several queries share the same labels, which saves a lot of memory at a small loss of quality.
lead.mlp-n-som-detektorer: Every neuron in the MLP is a small detector looking for a particular pattern. If it finds it, it adds something to the word’s notes.
lead.var-parametrarna-finns: The model has 8 billion learned numbers. Here you see where they sit: most of them in the MLPs.
lead.lager-for-lager: You can look at the notepad in the middle of the model and ask: what would the model guess if it stopped here? The answer sharpens layer by layer.
lead.forward-pass-som-kod: Here is the whole model as a short program. The comments on the right show the shape of the data after each line.
lead.lm-head-fran-vektor-till: After the last layer, the last word’s notes are turned into a score for every word in the vocabulary: how likely is that word to come next?
lead.sampling-temperature-top-k: The model produces probabilities, but something has to pick a word. A few knobs control how cautious or bold that choice is.
lead.den-autoregressiva-loopen: The model writes one word at a time. Each new word is appended to the text, and the whole procedure runs again.
lead.traning-next-token-loss: The model learns by guessing the next word across enormous amounts of text, seeing how wrong it was, and nudging its numbers a little. This repeats trillions of times.
lead.gradienter-och-minne: For every learned number, training works out which way it should be adjusted. Keeping track of all of that takes far more memory than just using the model.
lead.prefill-och-decode: A response is produced in two phases. First the whole question is read in one go, which is fast. Then the answer is written one word at a time, which takes longer.
lead.kv-cache-steg-for-steg: When the model processes token number 100, it needs the labels and contents of the previous 99. The KV cache saves them so they do not have to be recomputed every time.
lead.kv-cachen-pa-riktigt-en: Here a real small model compares the same step with and without a cache. The logits are mathematically equivalent; floating-point rounding can cause small differences.
lead.ett-decode-steg-med-shapes: Here is a single writing step in detail, with the cache included.
lead.hur-stor-blir-kv-cachen: The cache takes GPU memory for each token in every ongoing conversation. Here you calculate how much.
lead.vad-ligger-i-gpu-minnet: GPU memory is shared between the model's learned numbers and the cache for all ongoing conversations. What is left over once the model has taken its share decides how many can talk at once.
lead.varfor-batching-raddar: Reading in the model's 16 GB takes the same time whether you write for one user or a hundred. That is why it pays to write for many at once.
lead.latensmatt: Two times matter to the user: how long you wait for the first word, and how fast the rest flows out.
lead.kapacitetsplanering: With what you now know, you can work out how many users a GPU can handle, and how fast it is for each of them.
lead.kvantisering: You can store the model's numbers with fewer digits. That saves memory and makes the model faster, at a small loss in precision.
lead.tat-modell-eller-moe: Instead of one large MLP, a floor can hold many small ones and a switch that picks a few of them for each word. The model gets bigger but not slower per word.
lead.routern: The switch that picks experts is a small learned table. It scores each expert, and the best ones get the job.
lead.moe-i-inferens: All experts have to sit in memory, even though only a few are used at a time. That brings particular challenges when you run the model.
lead.attention-varianter: There are several ways to build attention that save memory. The difference shows above all in how large the cache gets.
lead.lang-kontext: The longer the text the model has to keep in mind, the more memory and compute time it takes.
lead.resonerande-modeller: Reasoning models are ordinary models that have learned to think out loud before answering. That costs many more writing steps.
lead.multimodala-modeller: Images can be turned into the same kind of vectors as words. Then the model reads them as if they were text.
lead.andra-arkitekturer: There are relatives of our model that are built for other tasks. These are the most common ones.
lead.en-requests-livscykel: Every question goes through a few states: it waits, it runs, it sometimes gets thrown out, and finally it’s done.
lead.problemet-fragmenterat-minne: If every conversation gets to reserve a lot of memory up front, most of it sits empty. That was the problem vLLM was built to solve.
lead.pagedattention: vLLM splits the memory into small boxes of 16 tokens and hands out one box at a time, exactly when it’s needed. No space sits reserved unnecessarily.
lead.prefix-caching: If two questions start the same way, for example with the same instruction, they can share the same saved boxes.
lead.continuous-batching: As soon as one conversation is done, the next in the queue takes its slot, instead of waiting for the whole group to finish.
lead.chunked-prefill-och-token: A very long question is split into pieces, so it doesn’t block everyone else waiting for their next word.
lead.samplern-och-structured: Last in every step, one word is chosen per conversation, with that conversation’s own settings.
lead.tensor-parallelism: When a model is too big for one GPU, every table is split across several GPUs. They each compute their own part and then reconcile.
lead.pipeline-data-och-expert: There are more ways to split the work across GPUs: by layer, by copy or by expert.
lead.speculative-decoding: A small, fast model guesses a few words ahead, and the large model checks all the guesses at once.
lead.flaggorna-och-vad-de-styr: vLLM is controlled by a handful of settings. Each setting maps to a concept you have already learned.
lead.starta-servern-och-las: Here is how to start vLLM and read what it says about memory.
lead.felsokning-symptom-och: Common problems, their likely cause and what you can change.
lead.hela-flodet: The whole journey of a question, from when it is sent to when the response streams back.
lead.riktningar-i-residual-stream: Inside the notepad, concepts seem to live as directions. Once you find the direction for a concept, you can measure how much of it is there.
lead.steering-och-ablation: Once you have found a direction, you can amplify or remove it while the model runs, and the model’s behavior changes.
lead.fran-hook-till-vikter-astra: The same intervention can be baked into the model’s tables permanently. Here we follow how such a weight edit is made.
lead.fusklapp: Everything that matters in one place, to look up when you need it.
lead.vidare-harifran: Suggestions for going further: read the code, experiment and build it yourself.

mod.11.lead: Tie it all together: common misconceptions, a cheat sheet with every formula and a final exam.
mod.11.desc: Misconceptions, cheat sheet, final exam and where to go next.
mod.11.goal.1: clear up the most common misconceptions
mod.11.goal.2: find every formula and number in one place
mod.10.name: Interpretation
mod.10.lead: How do you find a behavior inside the model and change it — and what does the intervention look like in tensors?
mod.10.desc: Directions, steering, ablation and how the intervention is baked into the weights.
mod.10.goal.1: explain what a direction in the residual stream is
mod.10.goal.2: tell steering, ablation and weight edits apart
mod.10.goal.3: describe the intervention in terms of tensors
mod.10.key.1: Concepts are represented roughly as directions in the residual stream, found as the difference between the mean activations of two groups.
mod.10.key.2: x · r̂ measures, x + α r̂ steers, x − (x · r̂) r̂ removes.
mod.10.key.3: The same intervention can be baked into the matrices that write to the stream, without changing any shape.
mod.9.name: vLLM: memory and scheduling
mod.9.lead: A server must decide which work fits now and keep each request’s cached state available. Separate this scheduling problem from executing the batch.
mod.9.desc: Paged KV memory, prefix sharing, batching and the scheduler’s token budget.
mod.9.goal.1: describe the path from HTTP request to streamed token
mod.9.goal.2: explain PagedAttention, prefix caching and continuous batching
mod.9.goal.3: explain how a token budget shares a step between prefill and decode
mod.9.goal.4: identify the memory and transfer trade-offs of disaggregated serving
mod.9.key.1: The frontend (HTTP, text) and EngineCore (ids, GPU) are separate processes. The engine runs in steps: schedule, execute, update.
mod.9.key.2: KV memory is a pool of blocks of 16 tokens. One block table per sequence maps logical blocks to physical ones.
mod.9.key.3: Prefix caching: a hash chain over full blocks lets common prompt beginnings be shared.
mod.9.key.4: Continuous batching and chunked prefill: the batch is decided anew in every step within a token budget.
mod.9.key.5: The batch is flattened to [N_tokens, 4096]. Logits are computed only for the last token of each request.
mod.9.key.6: Tensor parallelism splits every matrix (two all-reduces per layer). Speculative decoding verifies several tokens per pass.
mod.8.name: Model variants
mod.8.lead: Same basic idea, different trade-offs. What separates the models, and what does it mean for whoever has to run them?
mod.8.desc: MoE, attention variants, long context, reasoning and multimodal models.
mod.8.goal.1: explain MoE and the difference between total and active parameters
mod.8.goal.2: compare MHA, GQA, MQA and MLA on cache size
mod.8.goal.3: say what long context, reasoning and images cost at inference
mod.8.key.1: MoE: a router picks top-k experts per token and layer. Memory is set by all the experts, compute by the active ones.
mod.8.key.2: Fewer KV heads (GQA, MQA) or a latent cache (MLA) means a smaller KV cache and therefore more users per GPU.
mod.8.key.3: Long context: the KV cache grows linearly, attention in prefill quadratically.
mod.8.key.4: Reasoning models have the same architecture but do many more decode steps.
mod.8.key.5: An image becomes hundreds of ordinary positions in the residual stream.
mod.7.name: Inference and the KV cache
mod.7.lead: How the model actually runs: two phases with completely different bottlenecks, and the cache that makes generation practically possible.
mod.7.desc: Prefill, decode, KV cache, memory, batching, latency and quantization.
mod.7.goal.1: tell prefill from decode and say what limits each of them
mod.7.goal.2: explain exactly what the KV cache stores and why it is correct
mod.7.goal.3: compute KV memory for a model and a workload
mod.7.key.1: Prefill runs T rows per weight read and often becomes compute-bound once T is large enough; short prefill can be memory-bound. Small-batch decode is usually memory-bound.
mod.7.key.2: The KV cache stores K and V per position, layer and KV head: 128 KiB per token in Llama-3-8B with bf16. Without cache quantization it is mathematically equivalent, apart from floating-point rounding.
mod.7.key.3: A decode step is matmuls against the weights (shared by the whole batch) plus attention against the cache (per sequence, growing with the context).
mod.7.key.4: Batching: the weights are read once for B sequences, so throughput increases almost linearly.
mod.7.key.5: The weights decide whether the model fits. The KV memory decides how many concurrent users fit.
mod.7.key.6: TTFT ≈ queue + prefill. ITL ≈ one decode step.
mod.6.name: Training and adaptation
mod.6.lead: Inference uses learned parameters. Training changes them using data, a loss and an update rule; adaptation changes which behaviours the model learns.
mod.6.desc: Loss, gradient updates, pretraining, instruction tuning, preferences and low-rank adaptation.
mod.6.goal.2: say why training is parallel across the sequence but generation is serial
mod.6.goal.3: explain why training often needs much more memory per parameter than bf16 inference
mod.6.key.1: The target is the same sequence shifted one step. All positions are trained in a single forward pass.
mod.6.key.2: The gradient has the same shape as the weight. AdamW uses two moments for adaptive updates and decoupled weight decay. A common mixed-precision budget is about 16 bytes per parameter versus 2 at bf16 inference, plus activations; implementation and sharding affect memory.
mod.6.key.3: Pretraining, SFT and RL change only the weights, never the architecture. A reasoning model runs like any other.
mod.5.name: Logits → text
mod.5.lead: The last vector becomes a probability distribution over the next token, one token is drawn, and it all starts over.
mod.5.desc: LM head, sampling and the autoregressive loop.
mod.5.goal.1: explain what logits are and why only the last position is needed
mod.5.goal.2: describe what temperature, top-k and top-p do
mod.5.goal.3: describe the loop and its stop conditions
mod.5.key.1: LM head: h [4096] @ W_U → logits [128256]. Only the last position is needed during generation.
mod.5.key.2: Temperature scales the logits, top-k and top-p cut off the tail, then one token is drawn.
mod.5.key.3: Generation is autoregressive: one forward pass per token until a stop condition is reached.
mod.5.key.4: Temperature 0 is greedy but not guaranteed to be deterministic on a server.
mod.4.name: Attention and the MLP
mod.4.lead: Inside the block: attention moves information between tokens, the MLP works on each token on its own. Here is every tensor and every weight.
mod.4.desc: Q, K, V, heads, RoPE, the causal mask, GQA, SwiGLU and the forward pass as code.
mod.4.goal.1: follow Q, K and V through attention with the right shapes
mod.4.goal.2: explain the causal mask, RoPE and GQA
mod.4.goal.3: explain what the MLP does and why it holds 70% of the parameters
mod.4.goal.4: read the forward pass as code
mod.4.key.1: Attention is the only place where positions exchange information: Q [32, T, 128], K and V [8, T, 128], scores [32, T, T].
mod.4.key.2: The causal mask: position i only sees 0..i. That is why K and V for old positions never change.
mod.4.key.3: RoPE rotates Q and K so that only the distance between positions matters.
mod.4.key.4: The MLP works per position: [T, 4096] → [T, 14336] → [T, 4096], and holds 70% of the parameters.
mod.4.key.5: 8.03 B parameters in total, about 16 GB in bf16.
